newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak coalition party warns against entry to NATO.
newsitem.headline: Slovak coalition party warns against entry to NATO.

text.p: The Slovak National Party (SNS), a junior member of the ruling coalition, warned on Sunday that eventual NATO memberhip could economicaly ruin the entire country.

"To make our army fully compatible with NATO forces would cost billions of crowns and this could ruin the entire state of Slovakia," Jan Slota, Chairman of the ultra-right SNS, said during a discussion on Slovakia's eventual NATO membership on the public Slovak Television.
"And who knows whether this is not their (NATO) real aim," Slota added.
"I do not want to accuse them of this (ruining Slovakia) but, in the end, this may be the aim."

Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's nationalist-populist coalition government, consisting of his Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the ultra-left Workers Party (ZRS) and the SNS, has declared membersip in NATO and the European Union as its top foreign policy priorities.
Meciar has repeatedly asserted he wants Slovakia to be one of the first of the former Soviet bloc countries to join the alliance.
But NATO membership has become a very sensitive issue inside the ruling coalition, were the HZDS supports the move and the two remaining partners have several times openly opposed integration.

Slota compared eventual deployment of NATO forces in Slovakia to the Russian military presence in then communist Czechoslovakia after troops of the Warsaw Pact, the communist bloc Russian-led military alliance, invaded the country in August 1968.
Russian troops only left Czechoslovakia in 1990, shortly after the communist regime was toppled in 1989 by the "velvet revolution" after 40 years in power.
"We do not know whether we can believe their promises that no foreign military forces will be deployed in Slovakia," Slota said.
He added the country must be carefull with NATO membership, arguing that "people still remeber the 'temporary' Russian military presence, which lasted for 25 years."
"Frankly said, once we are in NATO, there will be no more chances to make our own decisions...we will only be allowed to shut up and obey orders," Slota said.
The Slovak parliament last month approved a referendum on the country's NATO membership. President Michal Kovac must set the date for the referendum by March 16.

NATO member states are to hold a summit in Madrid in July to nominate the first candidates for membership from post- communist countries, and diplomats have said Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are most likely to be named.
Soon after the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Slovakia was considered to be among the top contenders for early entry into NATO.
But its chances have waned after the United States and the EU repeatedly criticised Bratislava for lagging behind in the development of democratic principles.
